Soft Lenses Not Working for You?

Understanding Rigid Gas Permeable Contact Lenses

Book AppointmentCall: (732) 978-9306

Rigid gas permeable lenses, often called RGP or GP lenses, are firm contact lenses made from a material that lets oxygen pass through to your eye. Because they hold their shape instead of molding to the eye like a soft lens, they can give especially crisp, stable vision, and for some eyes they work where soft lenses don’t.

If you’re wondering whether a rigid lens could help, start with a conversation. Call Academy Vision in Pine Beach at (732) 978-9306 and ask.

When Soft Lenses Fall Short

Soft lenses feel comfortable right away for many people, but they take on the shape of the eye beneath them. If the front of your eye is irregular, a soft lens follows those irregularities and vision may stay blurry. Very high astigmatism can be hard to correct fully in soft lenses, too.

A rigid lens keeps its own smooth shape, and a thin layer of tears fills the gap between lens and eye, evening out an uneven surface. Rigid lenses are often considered for:

  • Higher amounts of astigmatism
  • Keratoconus and other irregular corneas
  • Corneal changes after surgery or injury

What Rigid Lenses Do Well

  • Sharp vision. A firm, smooth lens surface gives many people crisper vision than soft lenses, particularly with astigmatism or an irregular cornea.
  • Durability. With good care, a rigid lens is replaced far less often than most soft lenses, and it won’t tear the way a soft lens can.
  • A fit made for your eye. Rigid lenses are made to precise measurements, so the fit can be fine-tuned in ways a standard soft lens can’t.

What a Rigid Lens Fitting Usually Involves

Fitting rigid lenses is more detailed than fitting soft lenses, and it often takes more than one visit. It generally includes:

  1. An eye exam, including a careful look at your eye health
  2. Detailed measurements of the curve and shape of the front of your eye
  3. Trial lenses, with the fit checked on your eye, often using a temporary dye and blue light that show the tear layer under the lens
  4. Lenses made to your measurements
  5. Follow-up visits once you’ve worn them for a while

Adapting, With Help Along the Way

Rigid lenses take some getting used to. Most people are aware of them at first, and comfort builds as wearing time gradually increases. A steady routine helps, since a long break can mean adapting all over again.

This is where an ongoing relationship with your eye doctor matters. Small changes to a lens’s curve, size or edge can make a real difference in comfort, and they come from follow-up visits and honest feedback.

Made to Your Measurements

Many soft lenses come in standard sizes and can be reordered by the box. Rigid lenses are different: they’re made to the measurements of your eyes, and how they move and settle has to be checked in person. That calls for a hands-on fitting and follow-up care, not just a box to take home.

Related Lens Options

Scleral lenses and ortho-k lenses are both made from rigid gas permeable materials, and Academy Vision offers both.

  • Scleral lenses: larger rigid lenses that rest on the white of the eye
  • Ortho-K: overnight lenses that gently reshape the cornea
  • Contacts for astigmatism: soft lenses that correct uneven focus
  • Contact lens exams: what happens at a fitting
Are rigid lenses uncomfortable?

They usually feel more noticeable than soft lenses at first, and for many people that fades as their eyes adapt. A lens that stays uncomfortable, or causes redness or pain, should be checked by an eye doctor rather than worn through.

How do I care for rigid gas permeable lenses?

Clean and store them only in solutions made for rigid lenses, following the routine your eye doctor gives you. Never rinse or store any contact lens in tap water, and replace your lens case regularly. Handle lenses over a towel or a sink with the drain closed, since a dropped lens is easy to lose or chip.

Can I sleep in rigid lenses?

Only if your eye doctor has prescribed them for overnight wear, as with ortho-k. Sleeping in lenses that aren’t meant for it raises the risk of eye infections.

Are scleral lenses the same as gas permeable lenses?

Scleral lenses are a type of gas permeable lens, but much larger. They vault over the cornea and rest on the white of the eye, holding a layer of fluid underneath, which suits some eyes that can’t tolerate smaller rigid lenses.

When should I take my lenses out and call an eye doctor?

Take your lenses out and contact an eye doctor promptly if your eye becomes red, painful or unusually sensitive to light, if your vision suddenly blurs, or if there’s discharge. For sudden vision loss, a curtain or shadow across your vision, flashes of light with a sudden shower of new floaters, a chemical splash or an object that has penetrated the eye, call 911 or go straight to an emergency room. Rinse a splashed eye with clean water right away, and leave a penetrating object in place.

Have Questions About Rigid Lenses?

If soft lenses haven’t given you the vision or comfort you want, it’s worth asking about your options. Call Academy Vision at (732) 978-9306 and tell us what you’ve tried so far.

We’re Right Here When You Need Us

Our Services at Academy Vision

  • Scleral Lenses »

    If you’ve had trouble wearing contacts in the past, scleral lenses may be a better option. These lenses are designed for sensitive eyes or more complex vision needs.

  • Orthokeratology (Ortho-K) »

    Ortho-k lenses are worn overnight and gently reshape your eyes while you sleep. By morning, you can see clearly without glasses or contacts. It’s a great option for kids on a myopia management plan.

  • Toric Contacts »

    If you have astigmatism, you may have heard that contacts won’t work for you, or tried a pair years ago that never seemed quite clear.

  • Contact Lens Exams »

    A contact lens exam is a little different from a standard eye exam. We take extra measurements to make sure your lenses sit properly on your eyes and stay comfortable throughout the day.

  • Same-Day Contacts »

    Whether you can leave a fitting already wearing new lenses depends on a few things: your prescription, the type of lens that suits your eyes, and whether that exact lens is available to try.

  • Multifocal Contacts »

    If you’ve started holding your phone or a menu at arm’s length to read it, you’re far from alone.
